tone_statements.quote: Le dagba est une langue à tons. Chaque syllabe est porteuse d’un ton et sert à des fins distinctives. Trois tons ponctuels sont identifiés en dagba : Le ton bas noté [`], le ton moyen [-] et le ton haut [´] La langue n’a pas à proprement de tons modulés. Mais ce que nous présentons comme tons modulés ne sont autres que la succession des tons ponctuels dans les dissyllabiques du type CVV ou CVVC. Ils sont au nombre de six dont trois montants et trois descendants. Tons montants : [`´] ; [-´] ; [`-] (BH), (MH), (BM) Tons descendants : [´`] ; [-`] ; [´-] (HB), (MH), (HM)
tone_statements.translation: Dagba is a tone language. Every syllable carries a tone, which serves distinctive purposes. Three level tones are identified in Dagba: the low tone written [`], the mid tone [-] and the high tone [´]. Strictly speaking the language has no contour tones; what we present as contour tones are nothing other than successions of level tones in disyllabics of the type CVV or CVVC. There are six of them, three rising and three falling. Rising: [`´], [-´], [`-] (LH, MH, LM); falling: [´`], [-`], [´-] (HL, ML, HM).
tone_statements.locator: p. 25, Première partie: Phonologie, Chapitre I 'Le tonème', Introduction
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (L, M, H) on the syllable, lexically distinctive, with rising/falling patterns analysed as level-tone sequences on CVV(C); tone also grammatical (deverbal nominalisation L->H, plural and demonstrative tone alternations).

sources.note: Demography/location only: 34,000 in CAR (Ouham: Batangafo, Kabo, Bossangoa), 10,000 in Chad (Grande Sido; Sarh); dialects none known; may be intelligible of Kabba [ksp].

sources.citation: Keegan, John M. n.d. [1989 data]. The Daba Language (synopsis of 1989 field notes from Gradjim Gobeti, Maikongo, south of Moissala, Chad; = 'Keegan 1989: Daba Word List. Ms.'). Morkeg Books, Sara-Bagirmi Language Project. 8 pp.
sources.note: §2 Phonological Notes, p. 1: inventory as Eastern Sara; on CVCV stems (tìbì, kòsó, känjä) 'the second vowel in each of these cases is pronounced markedly weaker than the first'; vowel length only in monosyllables. No use of the term stress/accent; the remark concerns vowel neutralization, not a stress rule.

sources.note: Full first-hand tonology: Dagba is a tone language, every syllable bears a distinctive tone; three level tonemes (bas, moyen, haut) established by minimal pairs (pp. 25-30), no true contour tones - the six rising/falling 'tons modulés' are sequences of level tones on CVV/CVVC (pp. 30-35, table p. 35); H is lowered after another H or M; nominal tone schemes by syllable type (p. 124ff); grammatical tone: deverbal nominalisation by tone change (L base -> H derived, p. 130), plural marker vowel M -> H, verb-initial k- deletion conditioned by the tone of the following vowel, demonstrative tone con…
